---
title: "Tokens, Embeddings, and the Context Window"
subtitle: "What the units of text are, what the vectors are, and what a finite working sequence implies"
---

*Prerequisites: none. `learn/how-created.qmd` gives the short version of
the first half of this page; this page can be read on its own.*

## 1. What this page adds

A language model does not operate on characters or words. It operates on
tokens drawn from a fixed vocabulary, converts each token to a vector of
numbers looked up from a learned table, and at generation time works
within a finite sequence of tokens called the context window. Each of
those three facts has consequences that are easy to get wrong: why a
model can stumble on spelling, why two occurrences of the same word are
not represented the same way inside the network, and why adding more
material to a prompt is not automatically helpful. This page goes through
the three in turn.

## 2. Why models use subword units

There are several ways to cut text into units, and the one mainstream
models use is a compromise between the extremes.

At one extreme are small fixed inventories. A character-level model uses
individual characters as its units: the inventory is small, but every
sequence becomes very long and each unit carries almost no information on
its own. A byte-level approach goes one step further and uses the 256
possible byte values as its inventory, which means any text at all can be
represented, with no "unknown" unit ever needed, at the cost of even
longer sequences. [S-28] When GPT-2 was built, its authors reported that
models working directly on bytes were not competitive with word-level
models on large datasets. [S-28]

At the other extreme are whole words. Each unit then carries a lot, but
the inventory has to contain every word the model will ever meet. It
cannot: new names, rare words, misspellings, and words from other
languages keep appearing, and anything outside the inventory has to be
replaced by a placeholder "unknown" symbol. A method proposed for machine
translation addressed exactly this by encoding rare and unknown words as
sequences of smaller **subword units**, so that the model could handle an
open vocabulary. [S-27]

The compromise most large language models use is a vocabulary whose
entries are pieces of words, chosen so that frequent words are single
pieces and rare words are built from several. The most widely known
procedure for choosing those pieces adapts a data-compression algorithm
called **byte pair encoding** (BPE): it starts from single units and
repeatedly merges the most frequent adjacent pair into a new vocabulary
entry. [S-27] The GPT-2 authors described BPE as "a practical middle
ground between character and word level language modeling," interpolating
between word-level units for frequent sequences and character-level
units for infrequent ones. [S-28] Many current tokenizers combine subword
units with a byte-level base or a byte fallback, so that anything not
covered by a subword piece can still be represented; implementations
differ in exactly how.

## 3. A BPE-style example

The procedure is easiest to see on a toy corpus. Suppose the training
text contained only four distinct words, with these counts:

| Word | Occurrences |
|---|---|
| `tall` | 6 |
| `ball` | 5 |
| `taller` | 4 |
| `tale` | 3 |

Start with every word split into single characters, so the vocabulary is
{`a`, `b`, `e`, `l`, `r`, `t`}. Count how often each adjacent pair of
units occurs across the corpus, weighting by word counts, and merge the
most frequent pair into one new unit. Repeat.

| Merge | Most frequent adjacent pair | Count | New vocabulary entry |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `a` + `l` | 18 | `al` |
| 2 | `al` + `l` | 15 | `all` |
| 3 | `t` + `all` | 10 | `tall` |

The first merge creates `al`, because `a` is followed by `l` in all four
words (6 + 5 + 4 + 3 = 18 occurrences). After that merge `al` is followed
by `l` in three of the words (15 occurrences), which creates `all`; then
`t` followed by `all` (10 occurrences) creates `tall`. Stopping after
three merges, the vocabulary has nine entries and the four words are
split as:

- `tall` → `tall`
- `ball` → `b` `all`
- `taller` → `tall` `e` `r`
- `tale` → `t` `al` `e`

The most frequent word has become a single token; the others are built
from shared pieces. A real run continues for tens of thousands of merges
over a far larger body of text, which is how vocabularies of the size
mentioned below arise. Several simplifications are in play: some widely
used tokenizers, including GPT-2's byte-level BPE, begin from bytes rather
than characters, while others use different base units or fallback
schemes; real tokenizers apply extra rules about spaces and punctuation
(§4); and not all of them are BPE. The counts above are recomputed by
`scripts/check_bpe_example.py`.

## 4. Spaces, punctuation, and why a token is not a word

Because the merge procedure only looks at frequency, it will happily
merge a word with the punctuation that often follows it. The GPT-2 paper
reports exactly this problem: their tokenizer was learning many versions
of common words "since they occur in many variations such as dog. dog!
dog?", wasting vocabulary entries. Their fix was to prevent merges across
character categories (letters with punctuation, for instance), with one
exception: spaces were allowed to merge with the word that follows them,
which improved compression at the cost of only minor fragmentation.
[S-28] In that tokenizer, a word with a leading space and the same word
without one are therefore different tokens, and punctuation is kept
apart from the letters next to it.

More generally, in many commonly used subword tokenizers, spaces and
punctuation influence the split, and the details differ between
tokenizer families. The same frequency-driven mechanism explains several
facts that surprise people the first time. A capitalized word and its
lowercase form are different character sequences and can tokenize
differently. A word at the start of a text (no leading space) and the
same word mid-sentence (leading space) can be different tokens. And an
ordinary word can be split in ways that have nothing to do with its
linguistic structure, because the pieces were chosen by frequency, not by
grammar. Different model families build
their vocabularies with different procedures and different training text,
so the same sentence can tokenize differently across models; GPT-2's
vocabulary had 50,257 entries, and BPE vocabularies of 32,000 to 64,000
entries were described as common at the time. [S-28]

Token IDs, finally, are indices into whichever vocabulary a model uses.
They are assigned when the vocabulary is built and carry no information
beyond "which row of the table."

## 5. Consequences for spelling, counting, and string operations

A model never receives letters. If a word is a single token, the model
receives one vector for it, and nothing in the input tells it how many
letters the word has or what the third one is. Any knowledge it has about
spelling has to have been learned indirectly, from text in which
spellings were discussed or words were broken up. Tokenization therefore
helps explain why spelling, character counting, and some string
operations can be awkward for language models. [S-35] It is not the sole
explanation for every such failure: a model can also simply have learned
a pattern imperfectly, and a task that is easy for a person can be
statistically rare in text.

## 6. Embeddings: the learned lookup table

Once text is tokens and tokens are IDs, each ID is replaced by a vector.
A vector here means an ordered list of $d$ real numbers, and every token
in the vocabulary gets a vector of the same length. The vectors are the
rows of a table $E$ with $V$ rows (one per vocabulary entry) and $d$
columns, and the conversion is a row lookup, $\mathbf{e} = E_{\text{id}}$.

The entries of $E$ are parameters, learned along with everything else.
The idea is due to an early neural language model, which associated each
word with a real-valued vector, expressed the probability of a word
sequence in terms of those vectors, and learned the vectors and the
probability function simultaneously; the table was "a $|V| \times m$
matrix of free parameters." [S-29] The transformer uses learned
embeddings in the same way, converting input tokens to vectors of a fixed
dimension. [S-30]

What structure do the learned vectors have? The same early paper gave the
reason any structure appears at all: the model generalizes because
"similar" words are expected to end up with similar vectors, and because
the probability function is a smooth function of the vectors, so a
sequence never seen in training gets reasonable probability if it is
made of words whose vectors are near those of a sequence that was seen.
[S-29] Training pushes tokens that occur in similar contexts toward
similar vectors, because that makes prediction easier. Two cautions
follow. Nearness in this table reflects learned statistical relationships
in the training text, which may or may not line up with a relationship a
person would name. And nothing guarantees that individual coordinates, or
particular directions, correspond to clean human-interpretable
properties; a row of $E$ is a list of numbers that turned out to be
useful, not a list of attributes.

## 7. Three things that are easy to confuse

The **token ID** is an integer index. The **token embedding** is the row
of $E$ that the index selects. Both depend only on which vocabulary entry
the token is. Every occurrence of the token ` bank` in every text the
model ever processes starts from the same ID and the same row of $E$.

The **contextual representation** is different. After the embedding
lookup, position information is added, because the transformer has no
built-in notion of order [S-30], and the vectors then pass through the
network's layers. Inside each transformer block, one mechanism, attention,
moves information between positions. [S-19] In the autoregressive decoder
this course is about, a position may use itself and the permitted earlier
positions, never later ones, so after several layers the vector at the
position of ` bank` depends on ` bank` and on what came before it. In
"the river bank" and "the central bank", the token ` bank` has the same
ID and the same initial embedding in both, and the different words before
it cause its later contextual representations to differ. That is the
difference between a lookup table and a network: the table gives every
occurrence the same starting point, and the network computes something
occurrence-specific from it.

At the output end, the representation at the last position is turned into
one raw score per vocabulary entry, which softmax converts into a
probability distribution over the next token (`learn/softmax-sampling.qmd`
covers that step). The whole pipeline is therefore vocabulary → ID → row
of $E$ → layers → scores over the vocabulary.

## 8. The context window

At generation time the model works on a finite sequence of tokens. That
sequence, everything the model can reference when producing its output,
including the output it has already produced, is the **context window**.
Its size is a fixed maximum number of tokens. Each generation step
predicts one token, which is appended to the sequence, and the next step
runs on the extended sequence. [S-07] The window is distinct from the
model's parameters and from the text the model was trained on: the
parameters were fixed when training ended, while the context is assembled
afresh for each request and holds whatever that request supplied. [S-31]

The size has grown a great deal. GPT-2 used a context of 1,024 tokens.
[S-28] Anthropic's documentation for the Claude API, accessed 2026-09-15,
describes context windows of up to one million tokens depending on the
model; that figure is product-specific and will change. [S-31] Whatever
the size, the sequence is finite, and once it is full something has to be
dropped, summarized, or left out before generation can continue.

## 9. What fills the context of an assistant

For a base model, the context is the prompt plus what has been generated.
For an assistant that has been given instructions and tools, the context
assembled for each model call can include, in general terms:

- instructions to the assistant (often called a system prompt);
- the conversation so far, both the user's messages and the assistant's
  earlier replies;
- text retrieved from a document collection or a search;
- definitions of the tools the assistant may call;
- the results returned by tools it has already called;
- files or excerpts made available for the task;
- the tokens generated so far in the current reply.

All of these are tokens in the same finite sequence, and they compete for
the same space. As one product-specific illustration: Anthropic's API
documentation, accessed 2026-09-15, states that everything in a request
counts toward the window (the system prompt, every message including tool
results and documents, and the tool definitions), that generated output
counts too, and that across a conversation each user message and
assistant response accumulates in the window. [S-31] Other products
assemble and manage context differently, and the same product may change
how it does so.

A small illustrative budget makes the arithmetic concrete. Suppose a
window of 100,000 tokens and a session in which:

| Item | Tokens |
|---|---|
| Window (illustrative) | 100,000 |
| Instructions | 1,500 |
| A file added to the session | 40,000 |
| Conversation so far | 12,000 |
| Tool outputs so far | 8,000 |
| Remaining | 38,500 |

The 61,500 tokens already used remain part of the logical context on
subsequent turns until the system removes, summarizes, compacts, or
otherwise stops supplying them, and the remaining 38,500 must hold every
further message, tool result, and generated reply. Implementations can
cache repeated input for efficiency, but cached tokens still occupy
logical context capacity. These numbers are invented to show the
accounting; real windows, and real token counts for a given file, depend
on the model and its tokenizer.

## 10. Practical consequences

**Irrelevant context competes with useful context.** Space is the
obvious cost: every token of unneeded material is a token unavailable for
something needed. There is also evidence that placement and volume affect
how well a model uses what it is given. One empirical study of long
inputs found that performance on tasks requiring a specific piece of
information was often highest when that information sat at the beginning
or end of the input and degraded significantly when it sat in the middle
of a long context. [S-32] Anthropic's documentation and engineering
guidance, accessed 2026-09-15, state that as token count grows, accuracy
and recall degrade, and recommend treating context as a finite resource
and finding the smallest set of high-signal tokens for the task; that is
one provider's statement about its models at that date, not a law.
[S-31] [S-34]

**Repeated material consumes capacity.** If the same file or the same
long instruction is added twice, it occupies twice the space and brings
nothing new. The accounting in §9 is unforgiving about this.

**Retrieval brings external information into the current inference.**
Since the parameters are fixed and the model's ability to access precise
knowledge stored in them is limited, a standard remedy is to retrieve
relevant text from an external collection and place it in the context, so
that generation combines the model's parametric knowledge with
non-parametric memory supplied at request time. [S-33] Retrieved text is
context, not training: it changes this request's inputs, not the model's
parameters.

**A larger window does not make selection irrelevant.** More room means
more can be included, but the evidence and guidance above are about what
happens as the included material grows. Deciding what belongs in the
context, and where, remains part of using a model well, at any window
size. [S-31] [S-34]

## 11. Common misconceptions

**"Adding a document to the conversation teaches the model."** It does
not. Supplying a document at inference time does not update the model's
parameters: training and post-training change parameters, while
instructions, retrieved text, tool results, and files change
inference-time context. [S-31] A product may separately retain the
conversation or the files, keep persistent memory or project state, store
information externally, and retrieve it into a later model call. Those are
behaviors of the surrounding system, not changes to the model's weights.

**"A token is a word, and the context window counts words."** A token is
a vocabulary entry, frequently a word fragment, and in many tokenizers
spaces and punctuation influence the split (§4). Token counts for the
same text differ across tokenizers, so a window size in tokens does not
translate to a fixed number of words.

## 12. Check your understanding

::: {.check-understanding}
<details>
<summary>Why do language models use word fragments rather than whole
words or single characters?</summary>
Characters give a tiny inventory but very long sequences in which each
unit carries little. Whole words give informative units but an inventory
that can never contain every word, so rare or new words become "unknown".
Subword units are the compromise: frequent words are single tokens and
rare words are built from shared pieces, which greatly reduces the
unknown-word problem; a byte-level base or byte fallback can additionally
guarantee that arbitrary text remains representable (§2).
</details>
:::

::: {.check-understanding}
<details>
<summary>The token ` bank` appears in two different sentences. Which of
the following are the same in both cases: the token ID, the initial
embedding, the contextual representation after the transformer's
layers?</summary>
The token ID and the initial embedding are identical in both cases, since
both depend only on the vocabulary entry. The contextual representation
differs, because the network's layers update each position using the
other positions in the sequence (§7).
</details>
:::

::: {.check-understanding}
<details>
<summary>You add a long file to a session and the assistant answers
questions about it correctly. Have the model's parameters
changed?</summary>
No. The file is in the context window, and each call reads it from there.
The parameters are unchanged. Whether the file remains available in a
later session depends on the product or surrounding system, not on
anything the model learned (§8, §11).
</details>
:::

::: {.check-understanding}
<details>
<summary>A model's context window is large enough to hold an entire
document collection. Is there any reason not to include all of it with
every question?</summary>
Yes. Every included token competes for the same finite space and is
re-sent on every turn, and there is empirical evidence that where and how
much relevant information is included affects how well the model uses it.
Selecting relevant material, for instance by retrieval, remains useful at
any window size (§10).
</details>
:::

## 13. Continue learning

- **Sennrich, Haddow, and Birch, *Neural Machine Translation of Rare
  Words with Subword Units*** (paper, arXiv:1508.07909; the abstract and
  the section describing the BPE procedure are enough for this page).
  Technical level. The original description of adapting byte pair
  encoding to build a subword vocabulary, with a worked merge example.
  Limitation: written for machine translation, before the byte-level
  variant and the space and punctuation rules described in §4.
  <https://arxiv.org/abs/1508.07909>

- **Radford et al., *Language Models are Unsupervised Multitask
  Learners*** (paper, the GPT-2 report; Section 2.2, "Input
  Representation", is one page). Technical level. Especially good for
  the concrete reasoning behind byte-level BPE and the punctuation and
  space rules, in the authors' own words. Limitation: describes one
  tokenizer from 2019; current tokenizers differ in details.
  <https://cdn.openai.com/better-language-models/language_models_are_unsupervised_multitask_learners.pdf>

- **Liu et al., *Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long
  Contexts*** (paper, arXiv:2307.03172; the abstract and figures carry
  the main result). Technical level. The empirical source for the
  placement effect in §10. Limitation: the models studied are from 2023,
  and the size of the effect varies by model and task.
  <https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.03172>

- **Anthropic, *Context windows*** (API documentation page, accessed
  2026-09-15). Practitioner level. A precise account of what counts
  toward one provider's context window, how turns accumulate, and how
  tool results and generated output are counted. Limitation:
  product-specific and revised over time; treat the numbers as of the
  access date.
  <https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/context-windows>

See `resources.qmd` for the complete list of sources used across this
course, with full source-map entries.
